docs.title: Nilabh Sharma — Data, AI & Delivery
docs.text:
AI for data engineers — explained in the language you already speak: pipelines, tables, grain, SLAs and lineage.

Most AI material is written for ML researchers or for complete beginners. This site is for people who have spent years moving, modelling and governing data — and want to understand where LLMs, RAG and agents actually fit, without the hype.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
Almost every "new" AI concept maps onto something a data engineer already knows:

AI concept What you already know The part that is genuinely new RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) An ETL pipeline whose sink is a vector index Retrieval is by meaning, not by key Embeddings A derived column It changes whenever the embedding model changes Chunking Choosing the grain of a table Wrong grain silently ruins answer quality Agents A DAG orchestrated by Airflow / Workflows The LLM decides the next task at runtime Evaluation Data-quality tests and reconciliation Outputs are probabilistic, so tests are statistical Guardrails Row-level security and data contracts They apply to generated text, not just stored data

docs.text: This site is written as I work through my own AI upskilling plan. Each article is published at the end of a two-week sprint, with what worked, what didn't, and what I'd do differently.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm Nilabh Sharma, a technical project manager and data engineer with 18 years of experience delivering data platforms, cloud modernization and enterprise integration programs — most recently Databricks lakehouse work for insurance, and large-scale application decommissioning for medtech.

I started this site to learn AI properly and in public: every concept explained through the lens of data engineering and delivery, with honest build logs.

  • LinkedIn

Disclaimer

Views are my own and do not represent any employer or client. Code examples are simplified for learning and are not production-ready.

docs.title: My journey: from engineer to delivery leader
docs.text:
2008 – today · How the scope of what I lead has grown, and what each stage taught me.

I've spent my whole career in data: first building it, then leading the people who build it, then owning the commercial and client outcomes around it. This page is the honest version of that path, including what I learned the hard way.

docs.text: 2008 – 2012 2012 – 2017 2017 – 2022 2023 – today Role ETL Developer → Senior Developer Project Consultant Technical Project Manager Senior Technical Project Manager Leading My own deliverables Delivery teams across EMEA A multi-year program across [N] pods A 29-person track (8 onsite, 21 offshore) Scope Data integration & reporting End-to-end integration systems 500-application portfolio $15M, 4-year delivery track Accountable for Quality of my pipelines and reports Delivery and client satisfaction Program outcomes and savings Plan, forecast, billing and margin 2008 – 2012 2012 – 2017 2017 – 2022 2023 – today

docs.title: Learning the craft
docs.text:
ETL Developer → Senior Developer · IT services organization ETLSQLPL/SQLShell scriptingTableau

I started in 2008 as an ETL developer, building data integration pipelines in SQL, PL/SQL and shell scripts, and the Tableau reports that sat on top of them. Over four years I grew into a senior developer role, trusted with the more complex integrations end to end.

Working at both ends, loading the data and building the reports people actually used, taught me how the whole chain fits together, and how a small problem upstream turns into a wrong number in front of a business user.

Leadership lesson: Know the work you'll one day lead. Having built pipelines and reports myself, I can still ask the right question in a review, spot an unrealistic estimate, and earn credibility with engineers.

docs.title: Leading delivery in front of the client
docs.text:
Project Consultant · Tata Consultancy Services, for a leading biopharma company · London, UK Enterprise data integrationReporting at scaleOnsite–offshoreStakeholder management

Five years onsite in London as the client-facing consultant for a leading biopharma company: owning the product backlog and end-to-end delivery of enterprise data integration and reporting, including dashboards used by 2,000+ sales people across EMEA. We grew the account by 10% while keeping customer satisfaction above 95%.

This is where I learned to run a project with the client in the room: managing expectations, saying no with data, and bridging an onsite team and an offshore team across time zones.

Leadership lesson: Trust is built by bad news delivered early. Clients forgive slips; they don't forgive surprises.

docs.title: Running a program at scale
docs.text:
Technical Project Manager, Big Data & Analytics · Tata Consultancy Services, for a global medical device OEM · Gurgaon, India Portfolio rationalizationLegacy decommissioningBig data modernizationAgile at scale

I led a five-year program to decommission 500 legacy applications, saving about $12M. We spent two years analysing a portfolio of [~1,500] applications to decide what could safely go, then delivered in waves: a 20-app pilot, then waves that grew to 120 apps each as we turned the process into a factory.

In parallel, we moved legacy architecture to modern big-data platforms and deployed 100+ automated pipelines.

Leadership lesson: Plan around the real constraint. In our case it wasn't engineering capacity; it was legal and business approvals. Once we planned around sign-off throughput, the waves ran on time. And the pilot is for learning, not for volume.

docs.title: Owning outcomes: data, AI and commercials
docs.text:
Senior Technical Project Manager · Tata Consultancy Services, for a leading insurance firm · Remote from Grenoble, France Databricks lakehouseAI-ready dataCommercial ownershipCustomer Journey Analytics

I lead a $15M, four-year delivery track with 29 people (8 onsite, 21 offshore). We built an enterprise Databricks lakehouse processing millions of daily customer interactions, designed as the foundation for analytics, machine learning and LLM use cases.

My role now goes beyond delivery: I own the plan, the monthly revenue forecast, billing, change control and margin, and I'm part of shaping the contract renewal.

Leadership lesson: A project is a commercial commitment first and a delivery plan second. Most delivery problems trace back to how the deal was estimated, so I start managing risk at sales handover, not at kickoff.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: I'm now investing deliberately in AI: learning in public on this site, building my first Claude agent, and applying 18 years of delivery experience to a question most organizations are struggling with: how do you take AI from a demo to something that runs reliably, safely and profitably?

docs.title: How my leadership has changed
docs.text:
• From output to outcomes: from "did we build it right" to "did it deliver the business value and the margin we promised".
  • From managing tasks to designing systems: entry gates, factories and forecasts that let a team run without me in every decision.
  • From my team to the whole deal: clients, partners, third parties and finance are all part of delivery.
  • From certainty to evidence: especially with AI, I now plan for experimentation and decide on evidence, not on optimism.

docs.title: Snowflake vs. AWS Redshift: a warehouse platform evaluation
docs.text:
Picking a cloud warehouse on feature lists is easy. Knowing what it will cost to run and operate is the hard part. This evaluation puts the two platforms side by side on architecture, how much operational work each needs, and costed estimates for production, development and test, so the decision rests on total cost of ownership rather than list price.

  • Outcome

    Snowflake was selected. Separating compute from storage, scaling without downtime and needing less tuning work gave it a lower estimated annual cost for the same workloads.

docs.title: The use case
docs.text:
An agent that profiles a Databricks table and drafts data-quality rules:

  1. Reads table metadata (schema, row count, partitioning)
  2. Runs profiling queries (null rates, distinct counts, min/max, pattern checks)
  3. Proposes DQ expectations with a rationale for each
  4. Flags columns that look like PII

docs.title: Success criteria (defined before building)
docs.text:
• [ ] Produces sensible rules for 8 of 10 test tables
  • [ ] Never runs a write or DDL statement (read-only credentials)
  • [ ] Every query it ran is logged and reproducible
  • [ ] Cost per table profiled is known

docs.title: Sections to write
docs.text:
• Design: the tools the agent can call
  • Build: minimal version with the Claude API / Agent SDK
  • Evaluation: results on 10 real tables
  • What went wrong, and what I changed

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. A pipeline you know: a DAG where you define every task and edge up front.
  2. An agent: the same building blocks (tasks = tools), but the LLM chooses which task runs next, based on the result of the last one.
  3. The loop: observe → decide → call a tool → read the result → repeat until done.
  4. What that breaks: reproducibility, runtime estimates, cost predictability, and testing.
  5. What you already know that still applies: idempotent tasks, retries, timeouts, least-privilege credentials, logging every step (lineage for decisions).
  6. When NOT to use an agent: if you can draw the DAG, build the DAG. Agents are for when the path genuinely depends on what you find.

docs.title: Practical rules (draft)
docs.text:
1. Agree the evaluation set and pass threshold with the business before building.
  2. Time-box experiments; decide go/no-go on evidence.
  3. Budget inference cost explicitly — it's opex that grows with adoption.
  4. Data readiness is the most common blocker. Check it first.

docs.title: LLMs for data engineers
docs.text:
Draft — publishing in Sprint 1

Outline below. Replace with the full article as you write it.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. What an LLM actually is — a function: text in, most-likely text out. No database, no memory between calls unless you pass it in.
  2. Tokens are your unit of volume — like rows or bytes. Pricing, limits and latency are all measured in tokens.
  3. The context window is working memory — think of it as the max payload of a single request. Everything the model needs must fit in it.
  4. Cost is capacity planning — input tokens × price + output tokens × price, per call, × calls per day. Estimate it exactly as you would compute cost.
  5. Temperature and non-determinism — why the same input can give different outputs, and why that breaks your usual testing habits.
  6. Where LLMs fit in a data platform — enrichment (classification, extraction), interfaces (text-to-SQL, Q&A over docs), and automation (agents).

docs.title: Key takeaway (draft)
docs.text: Treat the LLM as a stateless, probabilistic transformation step. Everything else — data, memory, access control, testing — is still your job.

docs.title: RAG is just ETL with a new sink
docs.text:
Sprint 2 article · ~8 min read

If you have built data pipelines, you already understand most of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The vocabulary is new, but the pipeline is familiar: extract from sources, transform into the right grain, load into a store built for the query pattern, and serve it to a consumer.

The consumer just happens to be a large language model.

docs.title: The problem RAG solves
docs.text:
An LLM only knows what was in its training data. It doesn't know your company's policies, your product catalogue, or last week's incident reports. You have two options:

  • Retrain or fine-tune the model on your data. This is expensive and slow, and it's stale the moment the data changes.
  • Look up the relevant data at question time and hand it to the model along with the question. That's RAG.

In data terms: instead of baking the data into the application, you join it in at query time.

docs.title: The pipeline, stage by stage
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Ingestion["Ingestion (batch / incremental)"]
        A[Sources<br/>PDFs, wikis, tickets, tables] --> B[Extract & parse]
        B --> C[Clean & chunk]
        C --> D[Embed]
        D --> E[(Vector index)]
    end
    subgraph Serving["Serving (per question)"]
        Q[User question] --> QE[Embed question]
        QE --> R[Retrieve top-k chunks]
        E --> R
        R --> P[Build prompt:<br/>question + chunks]
        P --> L[LLM]
        L --> ANS[Answer + citations]
    end

docs.title: 1. Extract: same as always
docs.text:
Connectors to SharePoint, Confluence, S3, ticketing systems and databases. You already know the problems: authentication, incremental loads, deleted records, and source owners who don't reply.

What's new: most sources are unstructured. Parsing PDFs, slides and HTML into clean text is often the hardest part of the project, and it's where quality is won or lost.

docs.title: 2. Transform: chunking is choosing the grain
docs.text:
You can't hand the model a 200-page manual. You split documents into chunks (say, a few hundred words each, often with some overlap) and retrieve only the relevant ones.

This is a grain decision, exactly like modelling a fact table:

  • Too coarse (whole documents): retrieval returns lots of irrelevant text, it wastes the model's context window, and answers get vague.
  • Too fine (single sentences): chunks lose their context. "It must be approved within 5 days" — what must?
  • Right grain: a self-contained unit of meaning, such as a policy section, a FAQ entry or a procedure step.

Also enrich each chunk with metadata: source, section title, date, owner and access level. These are your dimension attributes, and you'll filter on them.

docs.title: 3. Embed: a derived column
docs.text:
An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meanings get vectors that are close together.

Treat it as a derived column, computed by an embedding model:

chunk_id | source | section | text | embedding_model | embedding (vector)

The data-engineering consequence: the embedding depends on the model version. Change the embedding model and every vector must be recomputed. It's a full reprocess, like a breaking schema migration. Store the model name alongside the vector.

docs.title: 4. Load: the vector index is the new sink
docs.text:
A vector index is a store optimised for one query: "find the k rows whose vectors are closest to this vector."

Options range from dedicated vector databases to features in stores you already run, e.g. Postgres with pgvector, or Databricks Mosaic AI Vector Search. The Databricks version can sync incrementally from a Delta table, which is exactly the CDC pattern you already use.

docs.title: 5. Serve: retrieval plus generation
docs.text:
At question time:

  1. Embed the user's question with the same embedding model.
  2. Retrieve the top-k closest chunks, filtered by metadata (e.g. only the documents this user is allowed to see).
  3. Build a prompt: instructions + retrieved chunks + question.
  4. The LLM writes an answer grounded in those chunks, ideally with citations.

docs.title: A minimal version in Python
docs.text:
A deliberately simplified sketch that shows the shape, not production code:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env
MODEL = "your-claude-model-id"          # check docs.claude.com for current model names

# --- Ingestion (run as a batch / incremental job) ---
def chunk(text: str, size: int = 300, overlap: int = 50) -> list[str]:
    words = text.split()
    step = size - overlap
    return [" ".join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, len(words), step)]

def ingest(doc_id: str, text: str, metadata: dict):
    for n, piece in enumerate(chunk(text)):
        vector = embed(piece)            # your embedding provider (e.g. Voyage AI)
        vector_index.upsert(             # your vector store
            id=f"{doc_id}-{n}", vector=vector,
            metadata={**metadata, "text": piece},
        )

# --- Serving (per question) ---
def answer(question: str, user_groups: list[str]) -> str:
    hits = vector_index.query(
        vector=embed(question), top_k=5,
        filter={"access_group": {"$in": user_groups}},   # permission-aware retrieval
    )
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[{h.metadata['source']}] {h.metadata['text']}" for h in hits
    )
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=800,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "Answer using ONLY the context below. Cite sources in [brackets]. "
                "If the answer isn't in the context, say you don't know.\n\n"
                f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
            ),
        }],
    )
    return response.content[0].text

embed() and vector_index are placeholders for whichever embedding provider and vector store you choose. Anthropic's documentation points to Voyage AI for embeddings.

docs.title: What carries over from data engineering
docs.text: Data engineering practice In RAG Incremental loads / CDC Re-embed only changed documents; delete vectors for deleted documents Row-level security Filter retrieval by the user's permissions. Never retrieve what the user can't see and rely on the prompt to hide it. Lineage Keep source and section on every chunk so answers can cite them Data-quality tests Evaluation sets (see below) Schema versioning Version the embedding model and chunking strategy Freshness SLA "The index reflects source changes within X hours"

docs.title: Where the analogy breaks
docs.text:
Be honest about the parts that are genuinely new:

  • Retrieval is by meaning, not by key. There's no exact join. It's always "closest match", so you can get plausible but wrong chunks.
  • Output is probabilistic. The same question can produce differently worded answers. You test with evaluation sets (50–200 real questions with known good answers) and measure rates. A single assertion won't do.
  • There are two failure points. Bad retrieval (the right chunk wasn't found) and bad generation (the chunk was found but the answer is wrong) need separate metrics. Measure retrieval first, because most problems start there.
  • The context window is a budget. Every chunk you retrieve costs tokens (money and latency) and competes for the model's attention. More isn't better.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
RAG is a data pipeline with a probabilistic consumer. If you can build a reliable, governed, incremental ETL pipeline, you can build 80% of a RAG system. The remaining 20% is chunking, retrieval tuning and evaluation, and that's where to spend your learning time.
